items.title: The Two-Thirds Switch
items.question: Three doors hide one car and two goats. You pick a door, the knowing host opens a different door revealing a goat, and you switch. Your winning chance is 2/3.
items.correctExplanation: True. Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time; in the other 2/3 the host's forced reveal leaves the car behind the remaining door. Switching collects all of that 2/3.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, it is true. Count the three equally likely car positions: switching wins in two of them and loses in one. The reveal doesn't split 1/3–1/3 into 1/2–1/2 — it concentrates the 2/3 onto the door you can switch to.
items.lessonContent:
Count positions, not doors standing open.
The host's forced move transfers probability to one door.
'Feels fifty-fifty' is the famous illusion here.
Enumerate all cases before trusting symmetry.
Share this: deal three cards and play ten rounds of switch.

items.title: The Loyal Door
items.question: In the classic setup, refusing to switch and staying with your first pick wins with probability 1/3.
items.correctExplanation: True. Staying wins exactly when the first pick was right, which happens 1/3 of the time. Loyalty to a guess is never rewarded by the math.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Staying can only win if the original guess hit the car — a 1-in-3 event the reveal cannot improve. Everything the host does afterward is irrelevant to the staying player.
items.lessonContent:
Staying freezes your odds at the first guess.
Later information helps only players who use it.
Loyalty to a pick is sunk-cost in disguise.
Separate the decision's two branches and score each.
Share this: ask a friend what staying wins before revealing the answer.

items.title: The Even Split
items.question: Once the host reveals a goat, two doors remain, so each must now hold the car with probability 1/2.
items.correctExplanation: False — the classic trap. The two survivors are not symmetric: your door was picked blind (1/3) while the other survived a knowledgeable filter (2/3). Counting doors is not counting probability.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Two doors remaining does not mean two equal chances. Your door keeps its original 1/3; the host's filtering loads the other with 2/3. Symmetry must be earned by the process, never assumed from the scenery.
items.lessonContent:
Equal counts of options never imply equal odds.
Ask how each survivor reached the final two.
Filtering processes load probability unevenly.
Scenery symmetry is the oldest trap in probability.
Share this: catch one 'two options so fifty-fifty' error this week.

items.title: The Hundred Doors
items.question: With 100 doors, you pick one, the knowing host opens 98 goats, and you switch to the last door. Your winning chance is 99/100.
items.correctExplanation: True. Your pick is right 1/100; the host's 98 forced reveals funnel the other 99/100 onto the survivor. Bigger stages make the mechanism obvious.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Scale is the intuition pump: nobody believes their blind 1-in-100 guess beats the door that survived 98 deliberate reveals. The 3-door game runs the identical logic at smaller scale.
items.lessonContent:
Scale up thought experiments until intuition surrenders.
Ninety-eight forced reveals visualize the filtering.
Small cases hide mechanisms that large ones expose.
Trust the scaled version, then port the logic back.
Share this: explain the 100-door version to end a debate.

items.title: The Knowing Host
items.question: The 2/3 switching advantage depends on the host knowing where the car is and deliberately avoiding it.
items.correctExplanation: True. Knowledge plus the rule 'never reveal the car' is what filters probability onto one door. An ignorant host breaks the machine entirely.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The host's knowledge is the engine: deliberate avoidance of the car concentrates the odds. Remove the knowledge and the famous result evaporates — the ritual looks identical but the math differs.
items.lessonContent:
Assumptions about knowledge carry the whole result.
Rituals can look identical while the math differs.
'Knowing' versus 'random' is the load-bearing distinction.
State the host's knowledge before computing anything.
Share this: replay the game with an ignorant host and compare.

items.title: The Random Reveal
items.question: If the host opens a remaining door at random (knowing nothing) and happens to reveal a goat, switching still wins with probability 2/3.
items.correctExplanation: False. A random reveal that happens to show a goat leaves two symmetric doors — 1/2 each. Information content, not ceremony, sets the odds.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Randomness cannot filter: the surviving doors are symmetric given a lucky random goat, so switching gains nothing. Same stage, same goat, different knowledge — different answer.
items.lessonContent:
Knowledge filters; randomness merely samples.
Condition on the process, not just the outcome.
Lucky random goats carry no information.
Twin scenarios with different knowledge deserve different odds.
Share this: stage both host versions and feel the difference.

items.title: The Forced Goat
items.question: Whenever your first pick is a goat (2/3 of the time), the knowing host is forced to reveal the only other goat, so switching necessarily wins.
items.correctExplanation: True. With the car behind one of the two unpicked doors and one revealed as goat, the survivor must hide the car. The host's lack of choice is your gain.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Trace the 2/3 branch: first pick wrong, host has exactly one allowable reveal, the remaining door must hold the car. Forced moves transfer certainty — follow the constraint to the win.
items.lessonContent:
Follow forced moves to their certain conclusions.
The 2/3 branch decides the whole game.
Constraints on others are information for you.
'No choice' for the host means a gift for the switcher.
Share this: trace the goat-first branch on paper once.

items.title: The Adversarial Host
items.question: Suppose the host offers the switch only when your first pick already hides the car. Then switching always loses.
items.correctExplanation: True. A host who cherry-picks when to offer the deal reverses the advice: the offer itself signals your pick was right. Rules about the offer are part of the game.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Selective offers leak information in reverse — being invited to switch means you already won. Real-world 'deals' work like this: ask why the offer exists before accepting it.
items.lessonContent:
Offers are evidence about the offerer.
Ask why this deal exists before taking it.
Selective invitations reverse naive advice.
Game rules include when choices are offered.
Share this: spot one real offer that signals its own trap.

items.title: The Coin Decider
items.question: You pick a door, the knowing host reveals a goat, and then you flip a fair coin to decide whether to switch. This strategy wins with probability 1/2.
items.correctExplanation: True. Half the time you switch (winning 2/3 of those) and half you stay (winning 1/3) — averaging to 1/2. Randomizing between good and bad advice dilutes to mediocrity.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Compute: 0.5 × 2/3 + 0.5 × 1/3 = 1/2. Coin-flipping between strategies averages their odds — decisiveness for the better branch beats dithering exactly.
items.lessonContent:
Mixed strategies average their branches' odds.
Randomizing between good and bad dilutes to mediocre.
Commit to the better branch, don't hedge it.
Weighted averages settle strategy debates fast.
Share this: compute one mixed strategy's average aloud.

items.title: The Doubled Chance
items.question: Switching exactly doubles your winning chances compared with staying (from 1/3 to 2/3).
items.correctExplanation: True. Staying holds the original 1/3; switching captures the complementary 2/3 — precisely double. Few real decisions offer a free doubling, which is why the result startles.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. The arithmetic is exact: 2/3 is twice 1/3. 'Doubling' sounds like hype until the case count confirms it — two winning positions for switching versus one for staying.
items.lessonContent:
Complementary probabilities sum to the whole.
'Exactly double' claims deserve exact verification.
Free doublings are rare — notice this one.
Fractions beat feelings for comparing strategies.
Share this: show someone the 1/3 versus 2/3 split visually.

items.title: The Improved Original
items.question: After the host reveals a goat, your originally picked door becomes more likely to hide the car than it was at first.
items.correctExplanation: False. Your door never gets touched by the process — it keeps its original 1/3 exactly. All the revealed information concentrates on the other unopened door.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Nothing happened to your door: no reveal, no filter, no new evidence about it. Information flows only where the host acted. Untouched options keep untouched odds.
items.lessonContent:
Information lands where actions happened.
Untouched options keep their original odds.
Reveals elsewhere don't bless your pick.
Track the flow, not the furniture.
Share this: point at your door and ask what changed about it.

items.title: The Three Prisoners
items.question: Three prisoners await pardon for one; the warden names one of the other two as doomed. The classic 'three prisoners' puzzle is mathematically the same situation as Monty Hall.
items.correctExplanation: True. One winner among three, a knowledgeable revealer naming a loser, and the question of switching — the structure is identical with robes instead of doors. Isomorphic problems share solutions.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Map prisoner to door, pardon to car, warden to host: same numbers, same knowledge, same 2/3. Recognizing isomorphisms lets one solution pay rent across many puzzles.
items.lessonContent:
Isomorphic problems share one solution.
Strip stories to structure: choosers, hiders, revealers.
Robes or doors — the math can't tell.
One mastered puzzle can pay across dozens.
Share this: retell Monty Hall as the three prisoners.

items.title: The Final Briefcase
items.question: A TV game with 26 briefcases, no knowledgeable host, and a final swap offer is mathematically identical to Monty Hall, so swapping must be favored.
items.correctExplanation: False. With cases eliminated by the player's own random picks and no filtering host, the final two are symmetric — swapping gains nothing. No knowledgeable filter, no advantage.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Deal-style games lack the engine: nobody with knowledge sculpted the survivors. Random elimination preserves symmetry, so the swap is exactly even. Lookalike rituals need engine checks.
items.lessonContent:
Lookalike games need engine checks.
Random elimination preserves symmetry.
No filter, no advantage — demand the mechanism.
Famous fallacies travel under similar costumes.
Share this: explain why the briefcase swap is exactly even.

items.title: The Ten-Door Stretch
items.question: With 10 doors, you pick one and the knowing host opens 8 goats. Switching to the last door wins with probability 9/10.
items.correctExplanation: True. Your blind pick holds 1/10; eight forced reveals funnel 9/10 onto the survivor. The pattern generalizes: N doors give (N−1)/N to switching.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Generalize the mechanism: initial pick keeps 1/N while the survivor collects (N−1)/N. Ten doors make the funneling vivid — eight deliberate reveals can't be meaningless.
items.lessonContent:
Generalize: N doors give (N−1)/N to the switch.
Patterns across sizes confirm mechanisms.
Funneling scales with every forced reveal.
Test rules at N = 10 before trusting N = 3.
Share this: run the 10-door version with cards.

items.title: The Dependent Choice
items.question: Monty Hall surprises people because the host's choice of which door to open depends on the contestant's first pick.
items.correctExplanation: True. When you pick a goat, the host has no freedom; when you pick the car, he chooses between goats. That dependence — his move reacting to yours — is the information channel.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Dependence is the engine: the host's allowable moves change with your pick, so his reveal reports on your pick's quality. Independence would mean no information; dependence means the reveal testifies.
items.lessonContent:
Dependence is an information channel.
'His move reacts to mine' is the sentence that dissolves the paradox.
Independence means no news; dependence means testimony.
Find the dependency and the mystery converts to arithmetic.
Share this: state the dependence in one sentence to a friend.

items.title: The Three-Hundred Nights
items.question: A contestant plays the classic game 300 times always switching. She should expect to win roughly 200 cars.
items.correctExplanation: True. Frequencies make probabilities tangible: 2/3 of 300 is 200. Long-run counts are what single-case odds mean.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Multiply: 300 plays at 2/3 each gives about 200 wins, give or take luck's wobble. Frequency framing ('200 of 300 nights') is the cure for single-case blindness.
items.lessonContent:
Frequencies cure single-case blindness.
'200 of 300' persuades where '2/3' puzzles.
Long runs reveal what single nights hide.
Translate odds into imagined repetitions.
Share this: convert one abstract odd into a 300-night story.

items.title: The Staying Harvest
items.question: Playing 300 times and always staying should also yield roughly 200 cars, since persistence pays.
items.correctExplanation: False. Staying wins 1/3, so 300 loyal nights yield about 100 cars — persistence pays the revealer's tax. Loyalty feels virtuous and costs exactly 100 cars here.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Staying locks in the 1/3 first-guess rate: roughly 100 wins per 300 plays. Persistence is a virtue everywhere except where the math charges it double.
items.lessonContent:
Persistence has a price where odds oppose it.
Virtues don't override arithmetic.
Score loyalty in wins, not in feelings.
100 versus 200 settles the romance of staying.
Share this: price one loyalty of yours in expected wins.

items.title: The Early Reveal
items.question: Picture the ceremony reversed: the host first opens one goat door, and only then do you pick between the two survivors. Your winning chance is 1/2.
items.correctExplanation: True. A reveal before the choice filters nothing about your pick — the two survivors are symmetric at decision time. Order of operations decides whether information exists.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Timing is everything: filtering only helps players who chose before it happened. Pick after the reveal and you face a genuinely even pair — no door carries the concentrated 2/3.
items.lessonContent:
Order of operations decides what information exists.
Filtering helps only those who chose before it.
Reversed ceremonies deserve fresh computation.
'Then you pick' resets every asymmetry.
Share this: stage the reversed ceremony with cards once.

items.title: The Informed Door
items.question: After the classic reveal, all the new information belongs to the unpicked unopened door, and none belongs to your original pick.
items.correctExplanation: True. The host's actions never touched your door, so its 1/3 is pristine; every bit of filtering evidence landed on the survivor. Information has an address — check where it was delivered.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Your door received zero host attention, so zero updating applies to it. The survivor absorbed the full reveal. Ask of any evidence: which options did the process actually discriminate among?
items.lessonContent:
Evidence has an address — find its delivery.
Undiscriminated options keep prior odds.
Updating applies where filtering happened.
'Who was tested?' beats 'what remains?'.
Share this: trace one reveal to its addressed door.

items.title: The Equal Ceremony
items.question: Because the host always opens exactly one goat door before offering the switch, the ceremony guarantees both final doors are equal.
items.correctExplanation: False. Fixed ceremony does not mean symmetric information — the rule 'never open the car' loads the procedure. Equal rituals with unequal rules produce unequal odds.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'Always opens one goat' sounds symmetric but hides the constraint that manufactures asymmetry. Ceremony is theater; rules are mathematics. Read the rules, not the staging.
items.lessonContent:
Ceremony is theater; rules are mathematics.
Fixed rituals can hide loaded constraints.
'Always does X' still needs the why.
Read procedures for asymmetries, not pageantry.
Share this: find one fair-looking ritual with loaded rules.

items.title: The Lucky Guess Boost
items.question: A contestant with a genuine psychic hunch about the car's door should still switch, because hunches cannot beat 2/3.
items.correctExplanation: False — a real edge changes the priors. If the hunch is genuinely better than chance, the first pick exceeds 1/3 and staying can win. The 2/3 result assumes a blind first pick.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Monty Hall's numbers assume random first picks; genuine information (even a calibrated hunch) updates the priors. Assumptions bound every result — change the input blindness and the answer moves.
items.lessonContent:
Results inherit their assumptions' limits.
Blind-pick math needs blind picks.
Genuine edges update priors legitimately.
State inputs before quoting outputs.
Share this: name one assumption behind a famous result.

items.title: The Host Must Choose
items.question: When your first pick hides the car, the knowing host chooses freely which goat door to reveal.
items.correctExplanation: False — that case is reversed. Car-first gives the host two goats to choose between; goat-first leaves him exactly one legal reveal. Freedom lives on the 1/3 branch, force on the 2/3 branch.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Check: pick the car (1/3) and the host selects between two goats; pick a goat (2/3) and only one reveal is legal. The asymmetry of his freedom is precisely what loads the survivor.
items.lessonContent:
Freedom and force swap across branches.
The 1/3 branch grants choice; the 2/3 imposes it.
Host freedom is itself evidence about your pick.
Branch-by-branch analysis beats blanket claims.
Share this: act out both branches with a friend hosting.

items.title: The Revealed Goat News
items.question: The host revealing a goat tells you nothing new, because everyone already knew at least one unpicked door hid a goat.
items.correctExplanation: False. Everyone knew some goat existed, but which door the host selected — forced or free — reports on your pick. Existence was known; the selection is the news.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'A goat exists somewhere' was indeed old news; 'the host opened this one' is fresh. Selection among knowns carries information — that is the whole paradox in one sentence.
items.lessonContent:
Selections report; existences merely sit.
'Which one' is news even when 'some one' isn't.
Old facts plus new choices equal updates.
Separate background knowledge from fresh signals.
Share this: explain the selection-is-news idea in one line.

items.title: The Numbered Survivor
items.question: Suppose you pick door 1 and the host opens door 3. The chance the car is behind door 2 is still 2/3, regardless of which specific door he opened.
items.correctExplanation: True. By symmetry between the two unpicked doors, the specific number carries no extra weight — the 2/3 attaches to 'the survivor,' whichever it is. Labels don't leak information here.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is true. Doors 2 and 3 were symmetric before the reveal, so conditioning on 'he opened 3' leaves door 2 at 2/3. Specifics matter only when the rules treat doors differently — here they don't.
items.lessonContent:
Symmetric doors stay symmetric after symmetric rules.
Labels carry no weight without rule differences.
Condition on processes, not on names.
'Whichever survives' inherits the full 2/3.
Share this: swap door numbers mid-game and watch nothing change.

items.title: The Single Loss
items.question: A player switches and loses one game. This single loss is evidence that the 2/3 switching claim is false.
items.correctExplanation: False. A 2/3 strategy loses 1/3 of the time by design — single outcomes cannot falsify a rate. Evidence lives in long runs, not anecdotes.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Losing once is exactly what 2/3 predicts for a third of games. Probabilistic claims are tested by frequencies across many trials, never by one vivid loss.
items.lessonContent:
Rates are tested by runs, never by anecdotes.
One loss is predicted, not disproof, at 2/3.
Vivid singles overweight against dull frequencies.
Demand samples before surrendering strategies.
